The Maestro · Part 8 · Phase 2 · 🧠 ML engineer hat

The Data Refinery

Phase 2 starts with what the machine eats. Maestro-1 needs about 10 trillion tokens (Part 3), and the quality of those tokens matters as much as the size of the model. This part builds the data refinery that turns raw web pages, code and partner tasks into a training mixture: where the data comes from and what Gopala may use, three filters with runnable code, deduplication, the mixture plan, how verified skills enter the data, and the records that let him answer "what did the model see?" a year later.

1. Mission log: weeks 14–36

Weeks 14–18 · Sources and rights
  • Lists every candidate source with its licence, terms and opt-out status; drops anything he cannot defend to a partner's lawyer.
  • Downloads public filtered web datasets as a starting point instead of crawling everything himself.
Weeks 18–26 · The refinery
  • Builds the filter → dedup → classify pipeline on the pre-emptible partition (Part 7), using spare GPU and CPU hours between Maestro-0 jobs.
  • Writes the three scripts in this part and runs them on samples by hand before trusting them at scale.
Weeks 26–36 · Mixture and records
  • Runs small "data ablations" (Part 9) to choose the mixture; freezes the 10T-token blend for the main run.
  • Every shard gets a manifest entry: source, licence, filters applied, hash.

2. Why data decides the model

  • Same compute, different data, very different models.
    • Hugging Face's FineWeb work showed that careful filtering and deduplication of the same Common Crawl source produced better models than earlier web datasets at equal token counts.
    • FineWeb-Edu, a 1.3T-token subset kept by an educational-quality classifier, did better again on knowledge and reasoning benchmarks.
  • Frontier labs say the same.
    • Meta's Llama 3 paper describes heavy investment in filtering, deduplication and quality classifiers, and a final mix of roughly 50% general knowledge, 25% maths and reasoning, 17% code and 8% multilingual tokens.
    • Its 405B model was trained on about 15T tokens.
  • For Gopala the data is also the moat.
    • Part 1's thesis: verified skills from real partner work are the one ingredient competitors cannot download.
    • The refinery is where that ingredient is cleaned, protected and blended in.

Where 10 trillion tokens come from (planned shares)

Web, filtered and deduplicated55%
Code, permissive licences20%
Maths and science8%
Multilingual web7%
Books and long documents5%
Synthetic, from verified skills3%
Verified skills from partners2%

Our planned mixture for Maestro-1 (see mixture.py below). Llama 3's published mix is shown in the text for comparison.

3. What he may use

  • Every source gets a row in a register before a single byte is trained on.
    • Licence or terms of use.
    • Whether the site's robots.txt or an opt-out signal excludes AI training.
    • Personal data risk.
    • Whether the source could contain partners' confidential code.
  • The rule: if he could not explain a source to a partner's lawyer, it does not go in.
    • Court cases and settlements over training data (see the site's law and the data wall article) make provenance a business risk, not only an ethical one.
  • Code is the most delicate source.
    • Only permissively licensed code, with licence detection per file.
    • Partner code is never pre-training data; partners contribute verified skills derived from tasks, under contract (Part 3).
SourceUse?Why
Public filtered web datasets (e.g. FineWeb)Yes, as a baseDocumented pipeline, published licence terms, opt-outs honoured upstream
Own crawl of selected domainsYes, limitedRespect robots.txt and opt-outs; identify the crawler
Permissively licensed codeYesLicence detected per file; copyleft excluded
Paywalled news and books without a licenceNoLegal risk outweighs value
Partner repositoriesNoOnly verified skills derived from tasks, under contract
Synthetic data from his own modelsYesGenerated from verified tasks, checked by the same tests

4. The refinery, stage by stage

From raw pages to training shards

🌐ExtractHTML → main text; drop menus and ads
🌍LanguageKeep target languages
🧹HeuristicsCheap rules (Gopher-style)
🔁DedupExact, then MinHash near-duplicates
🎓ClassifyModel-based quality score
🛡️Safety & PIIRemove personal data, toxic content
📦ShardTokenise, record manifest

Each stage is cheaper than the next, so the expensive ones see the least data.

  • Order matters for cost.
    • Cheap rules run on everything; the model-based classifier runs only on what survives.
    • In published pipelines such as FineWeb, the large majority of raw crawl is removed before training.
  • Every stage writes what it removed and why.
    • So a later surprise ("the model never learned X") can be traced back to a filter.

5. Filter 1: cheap rules

  • The Gopher rules (DeepMind, 2021) are still the standard first pass.
    • Document length, mean word length, symbol ratios, share of words with letters, presence of common English words, repeated lines.
    • They are fast, explainable and catch spam, menus and broken extractions.
quality_filter.py · Python 3, no dependencies
"""quality_filter.py — heuristic document filters in the style of the
Gopher rules (Rae et al., 2021), the first gate of the data refinery.

Each rule is cheap and explainable; together they remove most junk before
any model-based classifier runs. SAMPLE documents are written for this
article. Thresholds follow the published Gopher rules where they exist.
"""
import re

SAMPLE = {
    "tutorial": "To install the package, open a terminal and run the installer. "
                "Then create a configuration file in your home directory and set the "
                "path to your data. The tool reads the file on start-up and reports "
                "any missing values, so check the log after the first run. " * 3,
    "spam":     "BUY NOW!!! $$$ best price best price best price click here click here "
                "#### $$$ !!! ### deal deal deal $$$ ### !!! click click",
    "boilerplate": "Home | About | Contact | Login\nHome | About | Contact | Login\n"
                   "Home | About | Contact | Login\nCopyright 2026. All rights reserved.",
    "code_doc": "def area(r):\n    return 3.14159 * r * r\n# compute the area of a circle "
                "given its radius r; returns a float. Use it in geometry exercises "
                "and check results against a calculator before submitting work. " * 2,
    "short":    "Click to continue.",
}
STOP = {"the", "be", "to", "of", "and", "that", "have", "with"}

def rules(doc):
    words = re.findall(r"\S+", doc)
    n = len(words)
    alpha = [w for w in words if re.search(r"[A-Za-z]", w)]
    lines = [l for l in doc.splitlines() if l.strip()]
    return {
        "50 <= words <= 100k": 50 <= n <= 100_000,
        "mean word length 3-10": n > 0 and 3 <= sum(map(len, words)) / n <= 10,
        "symbol/word ratio < 0.1": n > 0 and (doc.count("#") + doc.count("...")) / n < 0.1,
        ">= 80% words have a letter": n > 0 and len(alpha) / n >= 0.8,
        ">= 2 stop words": len({w.lower() for w in words} & STOP) >= 2,
        "duplicate lines < 30%": not lines or 1 - len(set(lines)) / len(lines) < 0.30,
    }

def main():
    kept = 0
    for name, doc in SAMPLE.items():
        r = rules(doc)
        failed = [k for k, ok in r.items() if not ok]
        kept += not failed
        print(f"{name:12s} {'KEEP' if not failed else 'DROP'}  " + ("; ".join(failed) if failed else "passes all 6 rules"))
    print(f"kept {kept} of {len(SAMPLE)}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 quality_filter.py # on five sample documents written for this article tutorial KEEP passes all 6 rules spam DROP 50 <= words <= 100k; symbol/word ratio < 0.1; >= 80% words have a letter; >= 2 stop words boilerplate DROP 50 <= words <= 100k; >= 80% words have a letter; >= 2 stop words; duplicate lines < 30% code_doc KEEP passes all 6 rules short DROP 50 <= words <= 100k; >= 2 stop words kept 2 of 5

Five sample documents through six rules

Tutorialpasses 6/6 · KEEP
Documented codepasses 6/6 · KEEP
One-line pagepasses 4/6 · DROP
Spampasses 2/6 · DROP
Navigation boilerplatepasses 2/6 · DROP

Real output of quality_filter.py on documents written for this article.

  • What the run shows.
    • The tutorial and the documented code pass all six rules.
    • Spam fails four rules, navigation boilerplate fails four, and a one-line page fails on length.
  • What rules cannot do.
    • They cannot tell a well-written wrong answer from a right one, or a dull page from an educational one.
    • That is the job of the classifier in filter 3.

6. Filter 2: deduplication

  • Duplicates waste compute and teach memorisation.
    • The same press release on a thousand sites, mirrored docs, pages that differ only by a date.
    • Exact hashing finds identical copies; near-duplicates need fuzzy matching.
  • MinHash + locality-sensitive hashing is the workhorse.
    • Estimate the overlap (Jaccard similarity) of each document's word 5-gram set from a short signature.
    • Bucket signatures in bands so only likely pairs are compared, never all pairs.
minhash_dedup.py · Python 3, no dependencies
"""minhash_dedup.py — near-duplicate detection with MinHash + LSH bands.

Exact hashing misses pages that differ by a date or a menu; MinHash
estimates Jaccard similarity of word 5-gram sets cheaply, and banding
finds candidate pairs without comparing every pair. Documents are
written for this article. Standard library only; fixed seeds.
"""
import hashlib, itertools, random

DOCS = {
    "a": "the cluster uses three power feeds per rack so that losing one feed leaves four of six supplies running in every node",
    "b": "the cluster uses three power feeds per rack so that losing one feed leaves four of six supplies running in every node updated 2026",
    "c": "posted today: the cluster uses three power feeds per rack so that losing one feed leaves four of six supplies running in every node",
    "d": "gradient checkpointing trades extra compute in the backward pass for a large reduction in activation memory during training",
    "e": "a mixture of experts routes each token to a few experts so that total parameters grow while compute per token stays fixed",
}
K, PERM, BANDS = 5, 128, 32          # 5-word shingles, 128 hashes, 32 bands of 4 rows

def shingles(t):
    w = t.split()
    return {" ".join(w[i:i + K]) for i in range(len(w) - K + 1)}

def h(s, seed):
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.blake2b(f"{seed}:{s}".encode(), digest_size=8).digest(), "big")

def signature(sh):
    return [min(h(s, i) for s in sh) for i in range(PERM)]

def main():
    sh = {k: shingles(v) for k, v in DOCS.items()}
    sig = {k: signature(v) for k, v in sh.items()}
    rows = PERM // BANDS
    buckets = {}
    for k, s in sig.items():
        for b in range(BANDS):
            buckets.setdefault((b, tuple(s[b * rows:(b + 1) * rows])), set()).add(k)
    cand = {tuple(sorted(p)) for ks in buckets.values() if len(ks) > 1 for p in itertools.combinations(ks, 2)}
    print(f"{'pair':5s} {'true Jaccard':>12s} {'MinHash est':>11s}  candidate?")
    for a, b in itertools.combinations(sorted(DOCS), 2):
        j = len(sh[a] & sh[b]) / len(sh[a] | sh[b])
        est = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(sig[a], sig[b])) / PERM
        print(f"{a}-{b}   {j:12.2f} {est:11.2f}  {'yes' if (a, b) in cand else 'no'}")
    keep, drop = [], set()
    for a, b in sorted(cand):
        if sum(x == y for x, y in zip(sig[a], sig[b])) / PERM >= 0.7:
            drop.add(b)
    print("drop as near-duplicates:", ", ".join(sorted(drop)) or "none")
    # probability a pair with similarity s becomes a candidate: 1-(1-s^r)^b
    for s in (0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9):
        print(f"  P(candidate | similarity {s}) = {1 - (1 - s ** rows) ** BANDS:.3f}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    random.seed(0); main()
$ python3 minhash_dedup.py pair true Jaccard MinHash est candidate? a-b 0.90 0.93 yes a-c 0.90 0.94 yes a-d 0.00 0.00 no a-e 0.00 0.00 no b-c 0.82 0.89 yes b-d 0.00 0.00 no b-e 0.00 0.00 no c-d 0.00 0.00 no c-e 0.00 0.00 no d-e 0.00 0.00 no drop as near-duplicates: b, c P(candidate | similarity 0.5) = 0.873 P(candidate | similarity 0.7) = 1.000 P(candidate | similarity 0.8) = 1.000 P(candidate | similarity 0.9) = 1.000

Near-duplicate detection on five documents

0.93 / 0.94MinHash estimate for the two edited copies of a
0.90true overlap for both
2 of 5dropped as near-duplicates
0 of 7unrelated pairs compared

Real output of minhash_dedup.py.

  • Reading the output.
    • Documents b and c are the same text as a with a date or a prefix added; MinHash estimates their overlap (0.89–0.94) close to the true values (0.82–0.90) and flags them.
    • Unrelated documents score 0 and are never compared.
  • The tuning knob is the banding.
    • With 32 bands of 4 rows, any pair above about 0.7 similarity is almost certain to be checked; pairs at 0.5 are checked 87% of the time.
    • More rows per band make the filter stricter; more bands make it catch more.
  • A choice with consequences.
    • FineWeb's authors reported that deduplicating each crawl separately worked better than deduplicating across all crawls at once, because global dedup removed too much good data.
    • Gopala follows the published approach rather than inventing his own.

7. Filter 3: a quality classifier

  • Train a small model to score pages by how much they teach.
    • FineWeb-Edu used an LLM to rate a sample of pages for educational value, then trained a small classifier on those ratings to score the whole dataset.
    • Gopala does the same with a twist: a second classifier scores engineering usefulness (code explanations, debugging write-ups, design docs), because his clients are engineering teams.
  • Thresholds are chosen by ablation, not taste.
    • Train small models on data kept at several thresholds and compare them (Part 9's ablations).
    • Too strict a threshold removes diversity; too loose keeps junk.
  • The classifier is itself a risk.
    • It inherits the biases of whatever model labelled its training sample.
    • He keeps 1% of rejected data in a random audit set and reads samples every week.

8. Planning the mixture

  • The mixture is a set of shares that must add up to 10T tokens.
    • Each source has a limited number of unique tokens after filtering.
    • If the target share needs more tokens than exist, the source is repeated (more epochs).
  • How much repetition is too much?
    • Muennighoff et al. (2023) found that repeating data up to about four epochs costs little compared with fresh data, while much more repetition gives rapidly diminishing returns.
mixture.py · Python 3, no dependencies
"""mixture.py — plan Maestro-1's 10T-token mixture and check repetition.

A target share per source, the unique tokens available after filtering,
and how many times each source must be repeated (epochs). Repeating a
source a few times is mostly fine; many more starts to waste compute
(Muennighoff et al., 2023, "Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models").
Available-token figures are our planning assumptions, not measurements.
"""
TOTAL = 10e12
# source: (target share, unique tokens available after filtering)
SRC = {
    "web (filtered, deduplicated)": (0.55, 9.0e12),
    "code (permissive licences)":   (0.20, 1.2e12),
    "maths and science":            (0.08, 0.35e12),
    "books and long documents":     (0.05, 0.25e12),
    "multilingual web":             (0.07, 1.5e12),
    "verified skills (partners)":   (0.02, 0.02e12),
    "synthetic (from verified)":    (0.03, 0.15e12),
}

def main():
    assert abs(sum(s for s, _ in SRC.values()) - 1) < 1e-9
    print(f"{'source':30s} {'share':>6s} {'tokens':>8s} {'unique':>8s} {'epochs':>7s}")
    for name, (share, avail) in SRC.items():
        t = share * TOTAL
        ep = t / avail
        flag = "  <- heavy repetition" if ep > 4 else ("  <- repeated" if ep > 1 else "")
        print(f"{name:30s} {share:6.0%} {t/1e12:7.2f}T {avail/1e12:7.2f}T {ep:7.1f}{flag}")
    uniq = sum(min(s * TOTAL, a) for s, a in SRC.values())
    print(f"unique tokens seen: {uniq/1e12:.2f}T of {TOTAL/1e12:.0f}T ({uniq/TOTAL:.0%})")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 mixture.py source share tokens unique epochs web (filtered, deduplicated) 55% 5.50T 9.00T 0.6 code (permissive licences) 20% 2.00T 1.20T 1.7 <- repeated maths and science 8% 0.80T 0.35T 2.3 <- repeated books and long documents 5% 0.50T 0.25T 2.0 <- repeated multilingual web 7% 0.70T 1.50T 0.5 verified skills (partners) 2% 0.20T 0.02T 10.0 <- heavy repetition synthetic (from verified) 3% 0.30T 0.15T 2.0 <- repeated unique tokens seen: 8.17T of 10T (82%)
  • The finding that changed the plan.
    • The verified skills from partners would be repeated 10 times at a 2% share: far past the point where repetition helps, and a recipe for memorising partner-derived examples.
  • The fix he adopts.
    • Lower verified skills to about 0.4% of the main blend (about two epochs), and use them mainly where they matter most: the final annealing phase at the end of pre-training and post-training (Part 11).
    • Expand the synthetic share generated from verified tasks and checked by the same hidden tests, so the skill signal grows without repeating the same examples.
  • Only about 82% of the 10T tokens are unique in the plan.
    • That is normal for a start-up: it cannot crawl like a frontier lab, so code, maths and books are repeated around two times by design.

10. How verified skills enter the data

From a partner task to training data

🧩TaskReal engineering task from a partner, under contract
🤖AttemptMaestro-0 solves it in a sandbox
✅VerifyHidden tests pass; no regression
✂️AbstractStrip partner code; keep the reusable skill core
🔒ReviewLicence and confidentiality check
📦DataSkill library + annealing data + RL tasks

The same verifier that guards the loop (Part 1) guards the data.

  • Abstracting is the confidentiality step.
    • A skill core keeps the method ("how to bisect a flaky test") and drops the partner's identifiers, file names and business logic.
    • A check scans every skill for strings that appear in the partner's repository; any hit blocks it.
  • Three destinations, three different uses.
    • The skill library for retrieval at inference time (Part 1's H1).
    • A small share of annealing data at the end of pre-training (this part's mixture fix).
    • RL tasks with hidden tests for post-training (Part 11).

11. Synthetic data, carefully

  • Synthetic data can multiply a scarce signal.
    • Generate variations of verified tasks (new inputs, renamed APIs, harder edge cases) and keep only those that pass their tests.
  • It can also collapse diversity.
    • Models trained heavily on their own outputs can lose rare knowledge over generations, the effect described as "model collapse" (Shumailov et al., 2024).
    • His limits: synthetic data is generated only from verified seeds, always checked by tests, capped at a few percent of the blend, and labelled in the manifest.
  • More on the trade-offs in the site's synthetic data article.

12. Records: what did the model see?

  • Every shard has a manifest entry.
    • Source and snapshot date, licence, filters and thresholds applied, dedup run id, token count, content hash.
  • Why it matters later.
    • Evaluation contamination checks (Part 12) need to know whether a benchmark leaked into training.
    • Approvals (Part 14) and partners will ask what data trained the model.
    • If a source has to be removed, the manifest says which future runs must exclude it.
  • The pipeline itself is versioned.
    • A sketch of the batch job, using a datatrove-style library, is below. It was written for this article and not run.
pipeline.py · datatrove-style pipeline sketch · not executed for this article
# pipeline.py — the refinery as a batch job (sketch for a datatrove-style
# library; class names follow Hugging Face datatrove's documented blocks,
# but check them against the version you install).
from datatrove.executor import SlurmPipelineExecutor
from datatrove.pipeline.readers import WarcReader
from datatrove.pipeline.extractors import Trafilatura
from datatrove.pipeline.filters import LanguageFilter, GopherQualityFilter, GopherRepetitionFilter, URLFilter
from datatrove.pipeline.writers import JsonlWriter

SlurmPipelineExecutor(
    job_name="refinery-cc-2026-10",
    pipeline=[
        WarcReader("s3://maestro-raw/cc/2026-10/", glob_pattern="*.warc.gz"),
        URLFilter(),                       # blocklists: adult, malware, opted-out domains
        Trafilatura(favour_precision=True),  # HTML -> main text
        LanguageFilter(languages=["en"]),
        GopherRepetitionFilter(),
        GopherQualityFilter(),             # the rules in quality_filter.py
        JsonlWriter("s3://maestro-clean/cc/2026-10/"),
    ],
    tasks=2000, time="12:00:00", partition="exp",   # CPU-heavy: runs on the pre-emptible partition
    logging_dir="s3://maestro-logs/refinery/cc-2026-10/",
).run()

13. What the refinery costs

  • Mostly CPU, storage and time.
    • Extraction, rules and dedup are CPU work; the classifier needs some GPU time.
    • It runs on the pre-emptible partition and spare CPUs, so its GPU cost is mostly absorbed by idle hours in the main block (Part 4's capacity plan).
  • The bigger cost is engineering attention.
    • Weeks of reading samples, tuning thresholds and running ablations. Gopala delegates the reading to agents with a strict rubric and checks a random 10% himself.
Scenario
  • In the story, the refinery is ready in week 26 and the frozen blend for the main run in week 36, two weeks later than planned because the mixture fix needed a second round of ablations.
  • These dates are the story, not measurements.

14. Personal data and harmful content

  • Web data contains people.
    • Email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, names attached to private details.
    • He removes or masks common personal-data patterns with rules and a named-entity model, and drops pages from domains that exist to expose people.
  • Harmful content filters run before training, not only after.
    • Classifiers for sexual content involving minors (zero tolerance, hash-matching against known material through established services), extreme violence and hate.
    • The aim is not a sanitised model; it is not teaching it material no customer should ever receive.
  • Every removal is counted per source.
    • If a filter removes far more from one language or region than others, it is checked for bias before it stays.

15. Keeping benchmarks out of the training data

  • If test questions leak into training, scores mean nothing.
    • Benchmarks are on the web; a crawl will contain some of them.
    • The GPT-3 paper (Brown et al., 2020) checked for overlapping 13-word sequences between training data and benchmarks; n-gram overlap checks of this kind are still the standard first pass.
  • His procedure.
    • Before freezing the blend, scan every shard for long n-gram overlaps with every benchmark in the evaluation plan (Part 12) and with the partners' held-out tasks.
    • Remove matches; record what was removed in the manifest.
    • Keep a private, never-published task set that cannot have leaked.
  • The Evaluation Layer article on contamination covers why this is never fully solved.

16. A week in the refinery

DayWorkWho
MondayNew crawl snapshot and partner skills arrive; pipeline runs overnightAutomated
TuesdayRead 200 random kept and 200 random rejected documents per sourceAgents with a rubric; Gopala checks 10%
WednesdayAdjust a threshold if the samples show a problem; re-run affected shardsGopala
ThursdaySmall ablation on any changed sourceAutomated on the exp partition
FridayUpdate the manifest and the source registerGopala

17. Eight data mistakes

  • Training on everything downloadable and asking about rights later.
  • Deduplicating so aggressively that most good data disappears.
  • Trusting a quality classifier without reading what it rejects.
  • Repeating a small precious dataset many times at full share.
  • Letting partner code leak into pre-training data.
  • Using synthetic data without a verifier in the loop.
  • Keeping no manifest, so contamination cannot be checked later.
  • Changing the blend mid-run without recording it.

18. Delegation box

🙋 Gopala himself
  • Source register and rights decisions
  • Mixture choice and the verified-skill fix
  • Freezing the main-run blend
🤖 AI agents
  • Reading and grading rejected-data samples against a rubric
  • Licence detection triage
  • Writing manifest summaries
🤝 Bought, rented or borrowed
  • Public filtered datasets as a base
  • Open-source data tooling
  • A data-licensing lawyer for the register

20. The series

21. Reading the numbers

Primary / standard
FineWeb ~15T tokens; FineWeb-Edu 1.3T tokens; per-crawl dedup finding (Hugging Face). Llama 3: ~15T tokens; mix ~50% general, 25% maths and reasoning, 17% code, 8% multilingual (Meta). Gopher quality rules (Rae et al., 2021). Repetition up to ~4 epochs (Muennighoff et al., 2023). Model collapse (Shumailov et al., Nature 2024). MinHash (Broder, 1997).
Secondary ⚠️
None in this part.
